text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
Scottish doctor ROBERT LISTON, who performed the first operation in Britain on an anaesthetized patient, was born in 1794.
French chef de cuisine AUGUSTE ESCOFFIER, with the Carlton and Savoy hotels in London, was made a member of the Legion d'Honneur. He was born in 1846.
Tasmanian author JESSIE "TASMA" COUVREUR was born in 1848. Most of her novels were about the boring life she had led with her first husband - her second marriage was better.
Italian composer GIACOMO PUCCINI was born in 1858. He was the opera hitmaker with his works including "Madame Butterfly", "La Boheme", "Tosca" and "Girl of the Golden West".
Australian politician THOMAS LEY was born in 1880. He became the New South Wales Justice Minister and was later convicted of arranging the murder of the suspected lover of his mistress.
British journalist and satrical novelist EVELYN WAUGH was born in 1903. He wrote "Decline and Fall", "Brideshead Revisited" and "The Ordeal of Gilbert Pinfold".
British painter FRANCIS BACON, who began his career as an interior decorator in London, was born in 1909.
British cancer researcher, SIR RICHARD DOLL, who established the link between lung cancer and cigarette smoking, was born in 1912.
The anti-polio vaccine was developed by JONAS SALK, the American microbiologist who was born in 1914.
British singer and actress CLEO LAINE was born in 1927.

British singer and songwriter WAYNE FONTANA (GLYNN ELLIS) who launched his solo career in 1966, was born in 1945. His hit was "Pamela Pamela" (1966). United States singer with 'Dawn', TELMA HOPKINS, was born in 1948.
United Kingdom drummer STEPHEN MORRIS with 'New Order' was born in 1957.
** EVENTS **
1746 : An earthquake completely destroyed Lima and Callao in Peru.

1886 : The statue of Liberty was officially inaugurated by President GROVER CLEVELAND. The statue measuring over 49 metres tall was the largest gift ever given to the American people. It commerates the friendship between the peoples of France and the United States. French historian EDOUARD DE LABOULAYE suggested the idea at the end of the American Civil War. The statue was paid for by public donations in France. It was positioned on Liberty Island in the Upper Bay of New York Harbour.
1914 : The discovery of colour photographic was announced. GEORGE EASTMAN, who invented the Kodak camera in 1888, went on to develop the colour process.
1923 : Turkey was proclaimed a republic and MUSTAFA KEMAL ATATURK became the first president. ATATURK and his Turkish Nationalist Forces ended the Ottoman Empire.
1939 : The German SS proposed that all Jews should be made to wear a yellow Star of David as identification.
1939 : Thirty-five miners died in a pit explosion near Dunfermline in Scotland.
1949 : Violinist GINETTE NEVEU was among 48 people killed when an Air France jet crashed en route to New York.

1952 : Former Australian Prime Minister BILLY HUGHES "THE LITTLE DIGGER" died at the age of 90. He became prime minister in 1915 and 36 years later he was still a senior minister. He helped found the Labor Party and died a Liberal.
1958 : Television cameras were allowed into Britain's parliament for the first time to televise the state opening.

1962 : The world breathed a little easier after the Cuban crisis was averted. Soviet leader NIKITA KRUSHCHEV told President KENNEDY that work on the missile sites in Cuba would be stopped. The US military had been on alert for a week, underlining KENNEDY's determiniation not to allow alien missiles on America's doorstep. The Soviets also agreed to a UN inspection of the missile site to ensure that work had ceased and that the missiles had been shipped back to the USSR.
1977 : British police appealed for help in finding a vicious murderer of women. The killer has been dubbed the "Yorkshire Ripper".

1988 : The Prince of Wales renewed his attack on modern architecture. In a BBC television programme Prince CHARLES conducted a royal tour of architectural black and white spots. The black spots included LONDON's inner-city convention centre and Paternoster Square. A spokesman for Birmingham council called the Prince's criticism "a stab in the back from someone in an ivory tower". Royal Institute of British Architects president elect, MAX HUTCHINSON, said the Prince's thinking was "strangely nostalgic and out of time with current architectural throught and criticism."
